sections.title: Quick answer

body: Both people can suggest several ideas in the same discussion. Training, familiarity and the task can shape how they participate.

In a fictional meeting about low sign-ups, either person might suggest changing the time, topic or outreach channel. Those possibilities are useful to explore. The shared letters cannot establish who will suggest more ideas.

When the group chooses an option, one consideration is whether it honours a commitment to participants. Another is whether the evidence and reasoning support it. Both considerations can shape the same decision.
### Why sharing a dominant does not make them the same type

In type dynamics, E places the dominant process outward. P identifies that process as perceiving and N identifies it as Intuition, so both share dominant Ne. Their judging auxiliaries face inward. F gives ENFP auxiliary Fi, and T gives ENTP auxiliary Ti. Both have inferior Si.

Within the model, Fi weighs whether a decision aligns with personal values. Ti checks whether the reasoning is internally consistent. In the meeting, either person can raise concerns about fairness or question a premise.
When a discussion stalls, name both questions: what the group wants to protect and what the evidence supports.
Either type can revise a plan after discovering a weak premise or an unfair consequence. The decision does not establish someone’s type.

The Foundation’s [type dynamics table](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-overview/) allows Te or Ti for ENFP’s tertiary Thinking and Fe or Fi for ENTP’s tertiary Feeling. This page uses Te and Fe. The dominant and auxiliary processes remain the same under those alternatives.
sections.title: ENFP and ENTP: what they share and where they part

body: The six fictional examples concern the same community column. Both people have the same sign-up data, three comments, deadline and decision rights.
The rows separate decision criteria from shared preferences and role assignments. Either person can use either consideration.

| Same situation | One consideration | Another consideration | Preference illustrated |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The team considers changing the time after low sign-ups | Does the proposed time honour the team’s commitment to include residents with limited availability? | Would the evidence and the same decision criteria support a time change in a comparable case? | T/F: impact and values versus consistent reasoning |
| A resident says a request went unanswered | What did the team promise, and what did the missing reply mean for the resident? | Would the same standard for a satisfactory response apply to comparable requests? | T/F: the person’s situation versus a consistent criterion |
| Both people can discuss the proposal before finalising it | Ask a collaborator what they make of the same feedback | Talk through the same feedback with a collaborator | Shared E: either may turn to external discussion |
| Both face the same deadline and can change the topic | Consider the effect on residents who already agreed to take part | Check whether the change addresses the problem according to the same criteria | T/F: impact on participants versus consistency of the reasoning |
| A question remains open when the proposal is due | Keep a provisional option open until the missing evidence arrives | Keep a provisional option open while agreeing when to revisit it | Shared P: either can leave room for new information |
| Both can review the same proposal in two rounds | Check whether it honours the team’s participation commitment | Check which assumptions the available evidence supports | Shared work: swap reviewers in the second round |
The same person can weigh both criteria in every row. Work requirements and available evidence also shape what they do.
sections.title: ENFP and ENTP in one minute

body: When working together, agree on when to stop generating ideas and what the team needs to verify before choosing one.
In a shared study task, ask who the proposal would affect and whether the rule still holds in a counterexample. Either learner can ask both questions.

In a fictional book group, friends want newcomers to feel comfortable speaking. They could show two invitation drafts to willing readers and ask whether they would prefer open discussion or an option to send questions privately.
At handover, list any people whose input is still missing and any assumptions that need checking. Give each item an owner and a deadline based on the work.
### ENFP and ENTP in one planning meeting: two ways of closing
In a fictional planning meeting, both organisers have the same sign-up data, the same three comments and the same authority.

They consider a piece about residents who have trouble using a public catalogue. One question is whether the topic serves the residents the column aims to include. Another is whether the evidence shows where the difficulty occurs. Either organiser can raise either question.

In the first review, one person checks the proposal against the team’s participation commitments and the other tests the claim against the evidence. Swap roles for a second review, then revise what the evidence or commitments require.
Assign the checks by time and familiarity with the work. The roles do not indicate a type.
### ENFP and ENTP: picking the conversation up when an argument escalates

In a fictional disagreement, one organiser questions whether the data support the claim. The other worries that the proposed revision would leave out newcomers. Either person could raise either concern.
Ask each person to restate the other’s concern. Then decide what evidence would change the claim and which commitments the revision must protect.
Who speaks or asks first can depend on the task, responsibility or deadline.
sections.title: ENFP and ENTP in work and relationships

body: Thinking and Feeling describe different decision criteria. Both types can reason carefully and experience emotion.
Training and responsibilities can affect how someone presents a concern. Reflect on the evidence and values that influenced a decision you were free to make.
Either type can revise a plan because it excludes someone or because a premise is unsupported.
In a review, assess the actual decision and work against the relevant criteria. A preference label does not establish professional ability.
sections.title: ENFP and ENTP: avoiding misreads

body: If results alternate between ENFP and ENTP, compare the questionnaire, version, language and scoring notes. Consider whether you answered from your own choices or from a role that required a particular approach.

Choose a low-stakes decision you could actually make. Write down which evidence and values mattered, what could have changed your view and what the task required. Use the notes for reflection, without scoring or assigning a type.
If the evidence cannot distinguish two explanations, leave the question open. Note what would help you revisit it.

comparison_public_projection_v1.summary:
ENFP and ENTP differ in one letter: ENFP prefers Feeling (F), while ENTP prefers Thinking (T). Both share Extraversion (E), Intuition (N) and Perceiving (P).

- **Extraversion (E):** attention and energy tend to turn toward the outer world.
- **Intuition (N):** connections, patterns and possibilities carry more weight when taking in information.
- **Perceiving (P):** both codes indicate an outward-facing perceiving process, with a preference for staying open to new information.
- **Feeling versus Thinking (F/T):** Feeling gives more weight to values and how a decision affects people. Thinking gives more weight to logical consistency and criteria that apply across cases. Both types can use both.

Using the convention on this page, ENFP is Ne–Fi–Te–Si and ENTP is Ne–Ti–Fe–Si. Both lead with extraverted Intuition (Ne). Their auxiliary processes differ: introverted Feeling (Fi) for ENFP and introverted Thinking (Ti) for ENTP. Sources vary on the tertiary orientation. The stack cannot predict ability, behaviour or compatibility.

sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
Both people can suggest several ideas in the same discussion. Training, familiarity and the task can shape how they participate.

In a fictional meeting about low sign-ups, either person might suggest changing the time, topic or outreach channel. Those possibilities are useful to explore. The shared letters cannot establish who will suggest more ideas.

When the group chooses an option, one consideration is whether it honours a commitment to participants. Another is whether the evidence and reasoning support it. Both considerations can shape the same decision.

### Why sharing a dominant does not make them the same type

In type dynamics, E places the dominant process outward. P identifies that process as perceiving and N identifies it as Intuition, so both share dominant Ne. Their judging auxiliaries face inward. F gives ENFP auxiliary Fi, and T gives ENTP auxiliary Ti. Both have inferior Si.

Within the model, Fi weighs whether a decision aligns with personal values. Ti checks whether the reasoning is internally consistent. In the meeting, either person can raise concerns about fairness or question a premise.

When a discussion stalls, name both questions: what the group wants to protect and what the evidence supports.

Either type can revise a plan after discovering a weak premise or an unfair consequence. The decision does not establish someone’s type.

The Foundation’s [type dynamics table](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-overview/) allows Te or Ti for ENFP’s tertiary Thinking and Fe or Fi for ENTP’s tertiary Feeling.
